branch_hypotheses.observable_divergence_signal: Increase in worker expression toward problem-solving language and reduced complaint concentration around weekend fairness.
branch_hypotheses.plausible_path: Worker frustration softens, HR frames resolution as fair process, conflict remains contained within site operations.
branch_hypotheses.trigger: Shift managers gain limited discretion to swap or rotate weekend assignments.

branch_hypotheses.observable_divergence_signal: More frequent worker complaints, stronger peer alignment among schedule-stability seekers, and upward conflict edge from workers to leadership.
branch_hypotheses.plausible_path: Managers enforce more rigidly, worker resentment rises, and trust in leadership declines faster than trust in direct supervisors.
branch_hypotheses.trigger: Regional director insists on strict weekend coverage with minimal exceptions.

branch_hypotheses.observable_divergence_signal: Attention stays high but mobilization readiness stalls as workers shift from informal venting to formal complaint channels.
branch_hypotheses.plausible_path: Some workers pause escalation while waiting for process outcomes; legitimacy temporarily improves even without immediate concessions.
branch_hypotheses.trigger: HR opens a structured review or listening process before final policy lock-in.

branch_hypotheses.observable_divergence_signal: Lower visible complaints combined with persistent low trust and high fatigue in worker cohorts.
branch_hypotheses.plausible_path: Public expression drops while private dissatisfaction remains elevated, setting up later morale or attrition effects rather than immediate confrontation.
branch_hypotheses.trigger: Workers perceive low chance of change and high dependence on existing employment.

endpoint_ledger.contradiction_notes: Delay is not a terminal organizational endpoint if quickly superseded by a final policy; later evidence must confirm prolonged provisionality.

realization_criteria: Worker public complaint activity remains limited or declines

Workers, shift managers, HR, and a regional director disagree on policy, fairness, and operational needs. uncertainty_notes: Source corpus is brief and high-level; specific company size, warehouse location, union status, and exact policy details are not provided.
No explicit timeline horizon or formal decision deadline is stated.
No evidence of external media, regulators, or public controversy at T0.

sociology_baseline.description: Actors are more receptive to nearby framing such as fairness-plus-coverage compromises than to absolute positions.
Workers may escalate visible complaint behavior if enough peers signal shared grievance or if weekend assignments intensify.
Some workers privately disagree but remain quiet due to dependency and fear of isolation.
Workers primarily discuss impacts with workers, managers with managers, reinforcing role-based interpretations.
Visible repeated coworker complaints are more likely than a single message to shift broader workforce expression.
Role identity as workers, managers, or leadership shapes fairness and legitimacy judgments.
Absent new schedule changes or meetings, attention could drift somewhat, but direct personal impact keeps the issue live.

sociology_prompt_influences.description: Weekend scheduling is likely interpreted through fairness, predictability, and burden-sharing norms.
Management-side messaging is likely to emphasize coverage, continuity, and warehouse throughput.
Employment and scheduling dependence may suppress overt worker expression relative to private dissatisfaction.
HR process quality may affect whether conflict channels into complaints, accommodation, or resentment.
